info.name: South Sudan
info.stripDate: Tuesday 22 December 2026 (voter registration not yet started)
system: A presidential republic of 10 states and 3 administrative areas, governed under the 2011 Transitional Constitution (as amended) and, since 2018, the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS), which set up a power-sharing transitional government. This would be the first election since independence in 2011: the transitional period has been extended three times, most recently in September 2024, when the vote was moved to 22 December 2026.

A candidate wins outright with 50% of the valid votes plus one; otherwise the two leading candidates meet in a run-off within 60 days. Candidates must be South Sudanese by birth, at least 40 years old and backed by 10,000 registered voters from at least seven states (National Elections Act 2012, amended in 2023 and 2026). The SPLM has nominated President Salva Kiir; at least five other politicians had declared or shown interest by early October 2026.

Amendments signed in September 2026 cut the National Legislative Assembly from 650 to 270 members and each state assembly from 100 to 58; administrative-area councils have 20 members. In its January 2026 plan, made before these cuts, the Election Commission split seats between geographic constituencies (60%), women’s lists (25%) and party lists (15%). Governors and the chief administrators of the administrative areas are also on the December ballot.

South Sudanese citizens aged 18 or over, of sound mind and listed on the electoral register (National Elections Act, section 33). There is no register yet: as of early October 2026 the Election Commission said no voter had been registered and that registration will be manual, in person and on paper, on dates still to be announced. Whether displaced people, refugees and the diaspora can vote was still undecided in April 2026.

In July 2026 Parliament ratified amendments to the peace agreement that move the census and the permanent constitution to after the vote, a sequencing the African Union envoy had backed in April; on 21 September the President signed matching changes to the National Elections Act. The sitting executive keeps full powers until a new president is sworn in. In mid-September the President replaced the Election Commission chair, Abednego Akok Kacuol, with its secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng Majok, without giving a reason; opposition and civic groups question the Commission’s independence.

On 22 September 2026 President Kiir dissolved the transitional government and the national legislature and installed a caretaker administration; an inter-party dialogue opened on 24 September was shunned by part of the opposition. SPLM-IO leader Riek Machar has been detained since March 2025 and is on trial with seven co-accused on charges including treason, which he denies. The UN reported armed clashes, a “crackdown on government critics” and about 7.8 million people in acute food insecurity in mid-2026, while civil servants often go months without pay.
actors: Governing party of President Salva Kiir, in power since independence. It has endorsed Kiir as its presidential candidate and took nominations on 5–9 October 2026 for national and state legislative seats, governorships and chief administrator posts.
SPLM-IO · SPLM in Opposition (Machar wing, acting chairman Oyet Nathaniel Pierino)

Main opposition signatory of the 2018 peace deal, whose leader Riek Machar is detained. In August 2026 it rejected the 22 December vote and the amendments behind it, saying “elections held outside the framework of the peace agreement would not bring the transition to a legitimate end”, and demanded security reform, transitional justice, political space, a permanent constitution and a federal system first.

Juba-based former wing of the SPLM-IO, registered by the Political Parties Council in late June 2026 as “a distinct, separate legal entity” for the elections. Rival SPLM-IO factions dispute the legitimacy of its leadership.

Party of veteran opposition leader Lam Akol. Back in Juba in June 2026, he said NDM would run if the vote is credible, with civic space, freedom to campaign and a public timetable (“election is a process. It is not an event”), and called the government “bloated” while public salaries go unpaid.

Party of former Vice-President Josephine Joseph Lagu Yanga, a member of the SSOA alliance with no armed wing. In June 2026 it announced its registration and said it will contest the December elections; its statement sets out no programme.

Alliance of opposition signatories of the 2018 deal, now divided: in June 2026 Vice-President Hussein Abdelbagi Akol urged voters to back Kiir, while the alliance’s spokesperson said SSOA had endorsed no candidate. In September SSOA rejected the election-law changes as adopted without adequate consultation (Reuters).
SSOMA · South Sudan Opposition Movements Alliance (Thomas Cirillo)

Armed groups that did not sign the 2018 deal, led by NAS leader Thomas Cirillo. In late September 2026 it called the dissolution of the government a “coup d’état”, “categorically” rejected the planned elections and called for a new comprehensive peace process at a neutral venue outside the country.
PCCA · People’s Coalition for Civil Action

Coalition of activists and civic figures. In October 2026 it called for an inclusive national dialogue before any vote, questioned the Election Commission’s independence, denounced interference in opposition parties’ leadership and restrictions on opposition figures, and urged targeted sanctions and non-violent action.
info.why: No party has published a programme for this vote, and the ballot is not yet known: party nominations were only opening in October and no voter had been registered by 7 October 2026. Only the governing SPLM has a record that can be coded across policy areas; the main opposition SPLM-IO (Machar wing) and the SSOMA groups reject the vote, and the parties preparing to run (NDM, PDM, IO Party, SSOA members) have taken public positions almost only on the conditions of the election. A fair comparison will become possible if parties publish manifestos or campaign platforms on the economy, security, services and land, and the Election Commission publishes the final list of parties and candidates.
